caption:
You're picnicking on top of 20,000 bodies in one of the most popular parks in Manhattan — and New York City itself was once traded away for a tiny island of nutmeg. 👀

Comment your guess for which fact surprised you most before you swipe ⬇️

1. Washington Square Park
Before it became a hub for musicians and students, Washington Square Park was a public execution site and a potter's field. An estimated 20,000+ people are still buried beneath the lawns.

2. Grand Central Terminal
Track 61 was used by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to travel secretly from Grand Central to the hotel Waldorf Astoria, hiding his polio-related mobility struggles from the public. It's still there, sealed beneath one of the world's most famous hotels.

3. Central Park
Every hill, lake, and forest in Central Park was hand-built in the 1850s. Buried beneath it are the ruins of Seneca Village, a thriving Black community demolished to build the park.

4. Empire State Building
The spire wasn't decorative — it was designed as a mooring mast for airships. The plan was abandoned after the Hindenburg disaster, and the mast became a broadcast antenna instead.

5. Brooklyn Bridge
The bridge's basement vaults stored wine and champagne for decades. In 2006, inspectors exploring them found a fully stocked Cold War-era bomb shelter hidden inside.

6. New Amsterdam
In 1667, the Dutch gave New Amsterdam (today's New York) to the British in exchange for Run, a tiny spice island in Indonesia. At the time nutmeg was worth more than gold — arguably the worst trade in history.

7. 6½ Avenue
Manhattan has a secret half-avenue. "6½ Avenue" is a real, signposted pedestrian passage running between 51st and 57th Street that most New Yorkers walk past without ever noticing.
